summary:
CyberEagles is a browser-based lunar survival game that teaches students how astronauts balance power, oxygen, water, food and radiation on the Moon. Players manage a base through a full 28-day lunar cycle: 14 days of sunlight and 14 of night. They grow carrots and potatoes, melt ice from a permanent-shadow crater, clean dust from solar panels, contact Mission Control with a simulated delay, and shelter from solar storms and meteoroid impacts.

The game connects to real NASA data. A server-side function queries DONKI (CME and SEP space weather) and the OSDR RadLab lunar radiation database, keeping the API key out of the browser. The first storm replays the real May 8, 2024 CME. Every data source is labeled on screen as live, archived or simulated, so players learn the difference between real measurements and game assumptions.

Built with Python, Pygame and PyGBAG, it runs in any browser with no install, and fact cards and a glossary explain the science behind each challenge.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

CyberEagles is a free, browser-based lunar survival simulator that turns real space-exploration challenges into a game. The player is a junior astronaut running a Moon base for a full 28-day lunar cycle (14 days of sunlight, 14 days of night). To survive, the player must keep health, food, energy, water, oxygen and radiation under control while managing a limited battery.

Core gameplay: growing carrots and potatoes, recycling water, melting ice collected in a permanently shadowed crater, cleaning dust from solar panels, exercising and sleeping, and contacting Mission Control (with a simulated radio delay). Six objectives define victory, and an 11-step guided tutorial introduces every system.

NASA DATA INTEGRATION

- NASA DONKI (CME and SEP): space-weather event counts from the last 30 days. The first in-game storm replays the real CME of May 8, 2024 (official alert 20240508-AL-012).

- NASA OSDR RadLab: the latest available lunar radiation measurement, shown on the in-game NASA Data panel (F1).

- A Vercel serverless function queries these APIs on the server, so the NASA API key is never exposed in the browser. If an API fails, the game falls back to archived data.

- Every value is labeled on screen as live, archived or simulated. Players see exactly which numbers are real and which are game assumptions (for example, radiation exposure factors and impact schedules).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game makes abstract mission constraints tangible: energy and oxygen are linked, armor protects from radiation but cuts solar power, and the lunar night demands stored energy. Players learn why real astronauts make these trade-offs. Fact cards and a glossary explain concepts such as lunar ice, electrolysis, regolith dust and space weather. Because it runs in any browser with no installation, it can reach students, classrooms and anyone with a phone or laptop.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Python, Pygame-CE, PyGBAG (compiles the game to WebAssembly), Vercel (static hosting and Python serverless function), NASA DONKI and RadLab APIs, Visual Studio Code. No special hardware is needed; it runs on a standard desktop or laptop browser.

CREATIVITY

We combined a cozy pixel-art survival game with real NASA datasets and a transparent "real vs. simulated" labeling system. Resource management mirrors real mission planning, and learning happens through play rather than reading.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: NASA data is context, not a physics driver, and archived data is never presented as live.

- Security: the API key stays server-side.

- Reliability: a fallback chain keeps the game working when external APIs are down or rate-limited.

- Accessibility: browser-only, English interface, guided tutorial, keyboard controls.

- Limitations: simulated radiation and impact models are educational simplifications, not medical or scientific predictions.
